analysis.one_liner: Bars states from taxing multinational corporations on their worldwide income.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Several states used a 'worldwide unitary' formula to tax multinational corporations based on the income of their entire corporate family, including foreign affiliates. This bill would have forbidden states from doing that, except by the company's own choice, and would have limited how states tax dividends from foreign subsidiaries. The effect would be a multibillion-dollar tax cut for multinational companies, with states making it up from other taxpayers. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Multinational corporations with substantial foreign operations and foreign income. Under the worldwide unitary method, states could tax a share of the income a company earned anywhere in the world, reducing the ability to shift profits to low-tax foreign affiliates on paper. Banning the method (except when a company unconditionally elects it) would let those companies keep income that states currently reach. Domestic-only companies that compete with multinationals would also benefit, because multinationals would pay less state tax and the playing field would tilt their way.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits states from imposing tax on any taxpayer on a worldwide unitary basis, unless the taxpayer unconditionally elects to be taxed that way [S3].
Expressly bars the unitary method against domestic corporations whose average U.S. payroll, property, and sales are less than 20 percent of their worldwide totals [S2].

Limits state taxation of dividends from foreign affiliates: a state complies if it excludes at least 85 percent of such dividends, or the portion bearing no federal income tax after the foreign tax credit [S2].

Preserves state taxing rights over shell arrangements, by still allowing states to tax foreign corporations that carry on no substantial economic activity or that make most of their sales or payments to related U.S. companies and pay little foreign tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments, and ultimately the residents and domestic businesses that would make up the lost revenue. The states that used the worldwide unitary method would collect billions less in corporate income tax from multinationals, and they would need to raise other taxes or cut services to balance their budgets. Domestic-only corporations that pay tax on all their income would remain fully on the hook, shouldering a relatively larger share of state tax burdens than before.
analysis.who_pays_short: State budgets and other state taxpayers

drawbacks.text: States lose a tool they used to reach profits shifted to foreign affiliates on paper; the bill's defenders argued the method double-taxes foreign income and deters foreign investment in the state, a cost an honest supporter would weigh against the revenue loss [S2].

The bill overrides state tax policy from Washington: the Constitution left state taxation of multinationals to the states and courts, and this federal prohibition would take that choice away from state legislatures [S3].

The bill reaches further than foreign income alone: its dividend rules restrict how states tax dividends from foreign affiliates, and its definitions treat some domestic corporations as foreign, complicating state tax codes [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes narrowly to multinational companies and their shareholders, while the cost falls broadly on state budgets and on everyone else who pays state taxes. There is a real argument on the other side — that taxing worldwide income can double-tax profits already taxed abroad and discourages foreign companies from locating in a state — but the bill as written simply removes state revenue without any replacement, making the cost to state residents the dominant effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the same day and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator William Roth of Delaware introduced the bill on June 7, 1989, with five cosponsors — two Republicans and four Democrats [S1].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that is the last action of any kind in its history [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill never left the Finance Committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State governments and ordinary state taxpayers kept a revenue tool they would otherwise have lost, and domestic-only businesses kept multinationals paying tax on the same basis. Multinational corporations lost the chance at a federal shield from state taxation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States, their taxpayers, and domestic-only businesses

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — one Republican sponsor plus two Republican and four Democratic cosponsors — and there is no record of party-line opposition because the bill never got a hearing or vote.

industries.note: The bill would have exempted their foreign-source income and foreign-affiliate dividends from state taxation under the worldwide unitary method, shifting the burden to other state taxpayers. Its gain came directly at the cost of state revenue.
States using the unitary method would have lost billions in corporate tax revenue they would have had to replace through other taxes or spending cuts.

These companies already pay state tax on essentially all their income; a federal exemption for multinationals would have made their relative burden heavier, so blocking the bill preserved a level tax base.
The bill did not shield every arrangement: it kept states able to tax foreign affiliates that exist mainly to route sales or payments to related U.S. companies and pay little foreign tax [S3].
